newsitem.title: UK: Britain's Woolwich poised for flotation.
newsitem.headline: Britain's Woolwich poised for flotation.

text.p: Woolwich Building Society will next week follow recent stock market debutantes Alliance & Leicester and Halifax and ditch its 150-year-old mutual status to become a bank.

Latest indications from bookmakers City Index suggest the Woolwich will have a market capitalisation of around 5.1 billion pounds ($8.5 billion), which would place it among the top 100 quoted firms, when it floats on Monday.
Around 2.5 million members of the building society, which was founded in 1847 in south London, will receive at least 450 free shares when it converts.
City Index on Thursday quoted the closing price of the shares on July 7 at a spread of 316-324 pence, lower than its opening quote last month when it stood at 327-337 pence.

A Woolwich spokeswoman said it would announce on Friday how many of its members -- eligible savers and borrowers with the society -- have elected to sell their shares through an auction process when it floats.
Analysts expect around 25 percent of the shares to change hands in the initial auction.

The announcement will be made on the stock exchange and the auctions to institutional investors would be held after the close of trading on July 7,8,9 and 10 with members receiving the average price achieved.
The value of their windfall would be known on July 11, she added. But at the mid-level quoted by City Index, the minimum share allocation would be worth just under 1,400 pounds.
Analysts have said they expected shares in Woolwich, which is Britain's fifth largest mortgage lender, to be valued at the upper end of comparable companies.

This would reflect "an attractively positioned customer franchise, an apparent willingness to consider consolidation proposals, and several opportunities to leverage currently below-par returns on equity", according to Salomon Brothers banking analyst John Leonard.
In a recent research paper on Woolwich, Leonard said the shares would have an estimated trading range of between 315 and 325 pence and recommended them as a hold at this level.

Both Alliance & Leicester and Halifax saw their shares valued at levels which far exceeded market expectations. Alliance & Leicester shares were quoted at 603.5 pence and Halifax's at 775 pence at 1215 GMT.
In both cases much of the squeeze on the share price was attributed to the need for institutions and so-called index "tracker funds" to hold the shares when they joined the FTSE-100 share index.

But analysts said because Woolwich shares were expected to be incorporated into the FTSE-100 at the next regular review on September 19, this period could reduce the immediate institutional buying pressure.
Further price increases could be driven by take-over speculation, with expectations of consolidation in financial services keeping the British banking sector rife with rumour.

Leonard said both Woolwich and Alliance & Leicester are of a size and business mix "that clearly could be acquired by the larger institutions or by a number of outsiders with UK retail financial services interests".

Even though both have take-over protection as a result of the Building Societies Act, this potential for take-over "clearly commands a valuation premium relative to institutions that a principally acquirers".
Earlier this week Woolwich chief executive John Stewart told the Financial Times the group hoped to hand back some of its capital at its annual meeting next spring.

But he played down the chances of Woolwich going on the acquisition trail in Britain. If a building society or life company did become available, it could result in an auction and push the price beyond what Woolwich could pay.
"Our prime consideration is shareholder value, so we don't intend to overpay," he said.
The FT said he had indicated prices were more reasonable in France and Italy, where Woolwich is keen to grow its mortgage operations.
